What Does the Market Say? It is no small task to adjust the flat rates for changes in port charges, bunker prices, and exchange rates. But is it necessary? At the end of the year when the new flat rates apply to voyages with a load date on or after January 1, the spot market fixtures are based on a Worldscale percent for the new or old rates. Guess what happens? When fixing on the 2005 rates, the Worldscale percent was higher to reflect the lower flat rate and vice versa. This adjustment therefore provides the owner with the same revenues for a given voyage no matter which flat rate is used. No doubt the discipline imposed by the annual process and constant updates keeps the system from developing inconsistencies over time. But not to worry - if and when inconsistencies develop, the market will respond accordingly.

text: For those of you around the world who could stay up late enough to watch President Bush's State of the Union on Tuesday, it was some great theatre. The President correctly pointed out that "America is addicted to oil", but fell well short of offering any type of real solutions that would actually move the United States closer to anything resembling energy independence. In summary, the President's principal aim is not to reduce demand for oil, but to "make our dependence on Middle Eastern oil a thing of the past." This 30 year mantra has been repeatedly uttered by nearly every president since the oil crisis in 1973. President Bush proposed several solutions, including reliance on technology to enhance gasoline mileage efficiency and greater production of ethanol. Imports of ethanol are currently prohibited as a gasoline additive as only domestically produced ethanol made from corn can be used. Ethanol in gasoline as a substitute for MBTE is viewed as a not so hidden subsidy for corn growers. The President proposes that ethanol made from agricultural wastes and non-agricultural crops be allowed into the gasoline stream. This would probably not raise the heckles of the corn lobby because ethanol from cellulose rather than sugar and grains is a technology under development. Furthermore since vapor pressure considerations limit the ethanol content in gasoline, no one need worry about a massive influx of ethanol from cellulose into the U.S. gasoline stream. The best part was that he proposed to accomplish all of this by spending the equivalent of about two VLCC newbuildings. Are Americans Addicted to Gasoline? Absolutely! The chart on the next page shows weekly gasoline consumption and gasoline prices since last summer. Gasoline consumption is calculated as the total of gasoline produced by domestic refineries, gasoline imports, and changes to gasoline inventories. A decrease in gasoline inventories adds to consumption whereas an increase in gasoline inventories reduces consumption.

The chart shows that for gasoline below $3 per gallon, automobile usage is independent of price. We drove more in the summer as gasoline prices rose because this was the time to take the family on a vacation. We drove less in the autumn as gasoline prices fell because the kids were back in school. However although hybrid car sales spurted and large sized SUVs sales declined, America's favorite automobile is still large sized SUVs. But price discounting on large sized SUVs was enough to send Ford and General Motors into the red.
The Only Way to Break an Addiction... ... is to raise the threshold of pain to a level that breaking an addiction is preferable to continuing it. People break the smoking and alcohol habits when their consequences overwhelm their enjoyment. With regard to gasoline consumption, there is only one threshold of pain that Americans will respond to- a hefty price increase. Considering that they did not respond to $3 per gallon prices last summer, prices between $4 or $5 will probably be necessary for people to begin changing their driving habits to cut the gasoline addiction.
The irony of the situation is that the President has a ready reason to raise gasoline prices. Economists call it internalizing an externality. The externality is the hundreds of billions of dollars being spent for oil security: the cost of the war in Iraq. If this cost were transformed into an oil security tax on gasoline, the addiction might not be broken, but certainly weakened. For reasons that must certainly escape Europeans who pay $6 or so for a gallon of gasoline, no American politician has the intestinal fortitude to even suggest an effective cure for an addiction. It's all a matter of palliatives today as it was yesterday as it most probably will be tomorrow- no politician intent on reelection is interested in a cure.

The Twelfth Annual Shipping Conference of the Hellenic and the Norwegian-American Chambers of Commerce was held in New York on February 7 th . This year's theme was "The Image of Shipping: Perception and Reality." As always, the event draws together one of the best cross-sections of industry leaders. This year's conference was no different. Image of an Industry The first session was on the "Image of Shipping" moderated by Michael Grey of Lloyd's List. As has been true for years, Mr. Grey pointed out that there is always room for improvement on the public image of shipping. The popular perception as portrayed by the media is that of vessels running aground or spilling oil. The reality of shipping's excellent record with regard to performance and safety and its role as the lifeblood of world commerce is generally unrecognized. Mr. Grey suggested a number of ways to improve the popular perception of shipping including stressing the industry's benefits to society, showcasing role models, and confronting issues that contribute to giving a bad impression. Hamish Norton of Bear Sterns talked about Wall Street's perception of shipping as an industry known for glamour and quick fortunes, but also one that has experienced low historical returns and is subject to severe revenue cycles. Wall Street investors have little understanding of customary practices in shipping; for instance relying on flags of convenience and operating in a way that reduces tax liabilities. This has created an aura of an industry with a low sense of responsibility. Another practice that turns investors away from shipping is the separation of operations and ownership. Investors instinctively distrust managements contracting ship operations to third parties. Investors simply don't believe that the traditional structure of shipping works for the long term.
The cure for this is for more shipping companies to go public. Investors make or lose money in deeply cyclical industries, but most cyclical industries are owned by the public. Public companies have management structures and behavior that reflect generally accepted standards, especially those reflecting potential conflicts between management and shareholder interests. Compliance with regulations in terms of audited financial reports, transparency of operations via annual and quarterly reports, and oversight by a board of directors have made shipping companies that have gone public in recent years an attractive alternative for investors, particularly those shipping companies with assets in the multi-billion dollar range. Train 4 at Atlantic LNG faced similar feedgas delays. In the middle of last year, operators were planning to start producing LNG to the tank in September 2005, implying first exports one month later in October (see LNGWM, May '05). But this was postponed several months due to ongoing upstream constraints coupled with a minor incident involving mercury contamination in the refrigerants. Even when the plant was ready to start producing, contractual issues delayed loading operations after the shareholders balked at lifting cargoes while the necessary agreements with the government of Trinidad & Tobago were still outstanding. "Train 4 was ready to produce in early November. By December it had been through the loading and commissioning exercises. But the offtakers refused to lift cargoes until the government agreements were in place," comments one insider, who points to this contractual impasse rather than the train's gas supply problems as the biggest impediment to early startup. The first cargo from train 4 finally left Trinidad on January 8 and the upstream situation has improved to the point where operators now expect to get something close to the full feedgas allotment of 800 MMcf/d by the end of February or early March. Train 4 has added another 5.2 MMt/y of production capacity, boosting total design capacity at the Point Fortin plant site to 15.1 MMt/y.
In contrast to these other projects, Oman's Qalhat LNG exported its first cargo more or less on schedule on December 12 while Darwin LNG shipped out its inaugural cargo a full month ahead of plan on February 14 (see related article below). The venture had been hoping to begin loading operations even earlier and Tokyo Electric Power Co moved the Pacific Notus into position off Australia's Wickham Point in January to lift the first cargo. When the shipment failed to materialize after five days, the Japanese company dispatched the vessel to other business. It was eventually replaced by the Kotowaka Maru , which set sail for Japan with the venture's inaugural cargo earlier this month. Another tanker is expected to arrive within a couple of weeks to lift a second cargo for Tokyo Gas, the Australian project's other major customer. Once it is up and running, Darwin LNG expects to load a cargo every ten days. This could enable the venture to sell several pre-contract cargoes to the two Japanese utilities prior to March 31 when its term contract commitments are due to begin.

text: Last year was a particularly bad one for technical glitches and industry players are hoping the setbacks won't be repeated in 2006. These were particularly severe at Egypt's Damietta plant, which tripped off-line repeatedly due to electrical problems that have now been resolved. But it was by no means the only producer with technical issues: Australia's North West Shelf experienced compressor shaft vibrations at train 4 in August and had to shut the facility down for 35 days while Atlantic LNG was dogged by recurrent mechanical troubles including freezing problems at its existing trains. And the difficulties extended to Qatar, where RasGas II labored to resolve startup issues with train 4 and Qatargas identified pinhole leaks in the scrub column on train 1. Indeed, the problems at Qatargas may entail the replacement of scrub columns on all three of its trains during scheduled maintenance later this year. On the shipping side, the problems with some vessels equipped with GTT membrane tanks have been a matter of concern. "From a performance perspective the industry is showing strain across the board," comments one company official. Others argue that the setbacks reflect the construction sector's seriously overstretched resources and the introduction of new companies into the business. Only time will tell if the problems experienced in 2005 are a one-off or a harbinger of more to come.

text: For the first time in 20 years we are seeing the re-emergence of the "Double Exponential." The Double Exponential occurs when energy consumption growth not only reflects exponential growth in population, but also exponential growth in per capita energy (or oil) consumption. By plotting world energy consumption along with world population, we can see that energy growth outpaced population growth until the oil crisis in 1973 (actually this relationship had been true for a long time previous to the oil crisis). Growth in both per capita energy consumption and in population boosts energy growth and hence the "Double Exponential" curve.

text: The Clean Air Act of 1990 started the ball rolling with regard to reformulated and oxygenated gasolines and their impact on air quality. These requirements were area- and seasonal-specific. Reformulated and oxygenated gasolines were intended to reduce hydrocarbon emissions that contributed to smog. Oxygenated gasoline was also intended to reduce carbon monoxide emissions during the winter. Reformulated and oxygenated gasolines were generally confined to urban areas while conventional gasoline was sold in the rest of the nation. On top of these Federal requirements, states could impose their own limits, creating a gasoline boutique in the United States where gasoline specifications varied by location and season. Although the Clean Air Act did not specify the type of oxygenate, the two leading candidates were ethanol and MTBE (methyl tertiary butyl ether). The corn lobby was successful in defining eligible ethanol as that produced domestically from corn (maize). The oil industry picked MTBE because it was a refinery product already in use since the 1980s to enhance octane ratings after the phase-out of tetra ethyl lead. Moreover, MTBE was less expensive than ethanol. Over the years MTBE found its way into the water table affecting water supplies. Environmentalist objections to MTBE began to grow, particularly in California. In early 2003 California banned MTBE as an oxygenate and asked for a waiver on Federal oxygen content regulations. Subsequently other states, New York and Connecticut, banned MTBE in gasoline and switched to the alternative, ethanol.

Ethanol is "splashed" into the gasoline stream at distribution terminals before shipment to service stations. Before the Energy Policy Act, ethanol was added in accordance with the requirements set forth in the Clean Air Act; now it is left to the discretion of oil companies on when and where to add ethanol. Ethanol is highly absorbent of water and shipping by pipeline is not feasible. Ethanol is normally shipped by railroad tankcar, which is relatively expensive. To reduce this expense, ethanol consumption might become more localized in the long term, but in the short term ethanol has a vital role to play in compensating for the removal of MTBE from the gasoline stream to maintain octane ratings. Thus, ethanol will remain a component in gasoline. As more ethanol is needed to replace MTBE, imports may be necessary that would require the building or expansion of ethanol import terminals. Generally speaking, ethanol imports are discouraged by high import duties 1 . However, a limited volume of ethanol can come from selected Caribbean nations under the Caribbean Basin Initiative (CBI) that can enter the United States duty free. This includes Brazilian ethanol reprocessed in CBI nations.

text: Black Sea VLCCs and Fuel Oil Transport Double hull tankers must be used for fuel oil movements in European waters. But double hull tankers also obviate the need for heating. Many fuel oil cargoes from Baltic Sea ports are carried to offshore locations in the North Sea for somewhat lengthy ship-to-ship transfers to load a VLCC. Alternatively, VLCCs can load fuel oil at a terminal in Rotterdam. Another terminal is under construction that will also be able to load VLCCs with full cargoes of fuel oil. Thus a VLCC discharging crude oil in one Rotterdam terminal can switch terminals to take on a full cargo of fuel oil. Delays associated with VLCC discharges of fuel oil cargoes were also once lengthy and costly affairs involving transshipment from Singapore and/or lightering in Southeast Asian waters. Two fuel oil terminals are being built in China that can directly accept VLCCs. A third terminal may follow. With these improvements in terminals, fuel oil couldn't be a better fit as a backhaul cargo for crude oil from the Arabian Gulf.

text: BP's refinery of Texas City was damaged by Hurricane Rita and was scheduled to reopen the first week of April, but will most likely do so later in the month. Similarly ConocoPhillips' Alliance refinery and Murphy Oil's Meraux refinery have yet to resume operations, but are expected to do so this month. Simultaneous openings of these major refineries could conceivably boost the crude demand by 775,000 barrels per day. Spring Cleaning Regularly scheduled maintenance on refineries in the US and Europe is also lowering utilization and therefore demand for incremental crude. Europe, similar to the US, is experiencing some additional unplanned outages. The seasonal maintenance in Europe is earlier in the year than in the US, yet capacity is not expected to fully resume until May. In the Pacific, refinery turnaround season is expected to begin in April and peak in June. The overall reduction in capacity due to maintenance is anticipated to be around 12% and largely concentrated in Japan. Price Pressure Traders and Wall Street are also creating pressure on the market as futures prices for crude for Brent and WTI have been higher than spot prices. This situation provides an economic incentive for traders to hold their physical positions as long as the premium is enough to cover acquisition and storage costs. Current oil prices have increased to near $70 per barrel, a level that many analysts consider a psychological threshold for market pricing. After reaching $70 per barrel there is suggestion that the next range in which oil will comfortably trade is $75 to $80 per barrel. But it is far from certain that these price levels will reduce demand.

text: With crude stocks are at a relatively high level, it is perhaps not surprising that the number of days of crude inventory is also rising. Since the beginning of the year the days coverage provided by the inventory has been increasing. The decrease in Worldscale rates in March through the second week of April may be an indication that the days of inventory will be going even higher, pushing the demand for incremental crude even lower. The Million Dollar Question The looming question for tanker owners is whether demand will be met by increased imports or a stock draw down. Crude stocks are high, but refinery utilization is expected to increase to meet strong demand. As crude stocks are outside the five-year historical average band, it is presumed that a draw down on stocks is imminent. If seaborne imports are to be on the decline in the next few months, the tanker market will definitely feel the repercussions. But if inventory levels remain constant, or even increase in order to take advantage of the shape of the forward price curve for crude, the tanker market is not likely to remain low for long. In summary, watch the crude market for the next signal of the direction of tanker rates.

Playing by the Rules Non-double hull vessels that were delivered in 1978 and 1979 must phase-out by their anniversary this year. By the end of 2010, the regulations state that ships built in 1984 or later must exit the fleet. However, the Condition Assessment Scheme (CAS) was established to extend the usable life of certain qualified ships until 2015, or the 25 years of life. The number of ships that are set to be phased-out by 2010 is relatively gradual and in line with historic scrapping activity. If younger non-double hull ships pass the tests from the CAS the bulk of the scrapping activity will be postponed until after 2010. Due to the relative age of the current fleet many of these ships will not be due to scrap until 2015. The answer to whether or not states are going to comply with the IMO is a combination of economics and politics. For several countries, it is in their best economic interest to continue to accept single-hull tonnage past the phase-out date. Of the total non-double hull fixtures in the past year, the majority trade from the Arabian Gulf to South Asia, intra-Mediterranean and intra-Southeast Asia. Whether or not the governments of the countries loading and discharging cargo decide to comply with IMO regulations remains up to speculation. What is interesting, is that our database actually records several fixtures on vessels that should have phased-out. Conclusion Higher demand for crude and products combined with the projected overall increase in ton-mile demand creates upward pressure on rates in the near term. The balance to the increases in the fleet that are expected in the next few years will be managed by increasing demand for tonnage, not the IMO phase-out schedule. In the long run, the phase-out can be credited with supporting rates, but mostly post-2015. It will be even more interesting to see over the next several years if vessels that should have phased-out continue trading.

text: One of the more counter intuitive conclusions is that the age of the vessels should have no bearing on whether or not it should continue to trade. Mr. Devanney's point is that a vessel, regardless of age, must be properly maintained. A poorly maintained younger ship can pose more of a threat than a well-maintained older ship. To assume a vessel life at construction of a set amount of years, say 25, intrinsically sets the ownership up for failure by lowering expectations. Ships should not be designed with a specific operating life in mind rather they should be built with the idea that they will operate as long as they are well maintained. Conclusion "The Tankship Tromedy" presents a candid look at the design and construction of tankers: the pitfalls, the conflicts and the successes. It is not light reading, but members of the industry, regardless of affiliation, would stand to benefit from such a read. Shipping experience has shown that it is far better for the industry to take the lead than for the political process to impose its will.

It's A Long Way From Baku...
Starting in Azerbaijan at Baku, the pipeline runs through Tbilisi, Georgia ending up at Ceyhan, a Turkish port on the eastern side of the Mediterranean. The pipeline runs just over 1,000 miles and the pipeline itself has a capacity of 10 million barrels of oil. The inventory holding cost of filling this pipeline is about $700 million at today's crude prices. It will take several months to reach throughput capacity of 1 million barrels per day, as enough pressure must be generated to move the massive amount of cargo. It is estimated that the pipeline will meet intended capacity by the end of 2006. ...And Even Longer to China The type of crude to be produced from the pipeline is relatively light and low in sulfur, similar to the crude produced in West Africa. The crude is expected to end up in refineries on the East Coast of the United States as well as Europe and even the Far East- particularly China. Due to proximity, some refineries in the Mediterranean will also be looking into these cargoes, although these refineries are typically designed for heavier crude.

This week in New York City, the 19 th annual Marine Money Week was the forum that exposed some disparities in thinking between tanker owners and Wall Street analysts on the future direction of the tanker market. From Tuesday to Thursday the conference addressed many topics pertaining to the current shipping markets in all sectors- LNG, dry bulk, chemical and crude.
It was Wednesday, however, that proved to be one of the most interesting days with the discussion "Oil Demand Growth - Can It Keep Pace With Supply?" This was moderated by CNBC's financial heavyweight Larry Kudlow, host of "Kudlow & Company." One of the points discussed amongst shipowners and Wall Street analysts was the impact of global events on current rates and hence the direction for future rates.
This conversation revealed a striking disagreement between Wall Street and public tanker owners. It has been a grievance of some owners that shares of their companies are selling at a discount to net asset value, especially in comparison to other industries. On the other side of the panel, some analysts maintained that the market will experience downward rate pressure in the future and by their estimations equity prices should be lower today.
The reality is that the benefits received from the cyclical and spot nature of the business are difficult to clearly convey to the equity markets. From the analysts' perspective, the anticipation for lower spot rates in 2006 led to a series of downgrades in the past several weeks.
The difference for 2006 from previous years, is that there is much more overall demand today for tonnage. More crude is in the market today than in prior years and vessels are employed for longer distances resulting in increased ton-mile demand. Future Appears Firm Strong market fundamentals of supply and demand indicate that we can anticipate higher rates in the balance of 2006. As always the market commentary and outlooks that arise from panel discussions have proven to be very interesting. The strong projections for the market made by top executives, including one owner's outlook that VLCC rates will return to over $200,000 per day in the fourth quarter, may prove to be a bit too optimistic. While many are certainly bullish on the tanker market, projections like these are certain to raise some eyebrows. Changes in crude supply have enabled the market to absorb more tonnage overall and perhaps rates have universally shifted upward as the market experiences a higher rate floor. July 7, 2006 The International Energy Agency (IEA)'s latest Oil Market Report forecasts worldwide oil demand to reach 84.9 million barrels per day (bpd) over 2006, a 1.5% increase over last year's 83.66 million bpd. One major feature of this outlook is the United States' limited participation in demand growth. This outlook shows US demand increasing by just 170 thousand bpd, or by 0.8% over 2005. Other OECD demand growth is also weak. By contrast, non-OECD demand grows by over 3%. This week we take a look at what this outlook means for tanker demand and charter rates.

Since Iraq's invasion of Kuwait and Operation Desert Storm that followed, in the early 1990s, rate volatility has remained high. With a tighter supply-demand picture in global oil markets, driven primarily by India, China and the United States, the impact of global conflicts on oil prices and rates has become even more apparent over the last several years. Poised for a Collapse? In past conflicts, escalation has led oil companies to bolster their crude inventories to counteract supply impasses. Tankers were hired for storage and oil hoarded for anticipated supply interruptions. Oil prices increased based on actual physical tightness and speculation of inconsistent future supplies. When conflicts subsided this surplus oil was released from storage tankers and into the global market. Excess crude in the market negatively impacted oil prices and increased tanker tonnage availability creating a decline in rates. Operation Desert Storm The graph above shows the inflation-adjusted price (based on the CPI) for Arab Light/Brent crude over the past 35 years. The spike in prices resulted from the compounded effects of the Iran hostage situation and the Iran-Iraq war. By 1980, these events interrupted reduce worldwide crude production by four million barrels per day. Charterers took on tonnage as a means of storage and filled up shore-side facilities. In addition, high demand countries like the U.S. undertook projects and legislation reform designed to curb excessive dependence on oil. Conservation measures took hold as consumption began to decline in consuming nations putting downward pressure on tanker rates. This decline was, however, not as significant as the decline in oil prices from $85 per barrel to $25 that would occur over the next 5 years. Could we be facing the same situation? Historically, the natural progression of strong tanker markets, which resulted partly from crude supply constraints, has been towards a decline in rates. Going forward in today's environment there are three potential scenarios: a conflict is resolved peacefully, a conflict is resolved violently, or there is a decline in crude oil demand. In the short term, if a conflict is resolved peacefully with no major supply interruption, rates and oil prices should most likely stabilize. If conflicts are not resolved and supply disruptions occur, rates and oil prices will remain relatively strong until conflicts are resolved. If demand declines, expect rates and prices to decline more quickly.
For now, we are certain that the demand side of the equation is not set to change in the near term and the escalating conflict in the Middle East in recent weeks has added increased fears of supply interruption. Under these conditions, expect tanker demand to remain high, along with rates for the balance of the year.

The condensate market is divided generally between an East and West market. On the eve of this Monday's OPEC meeting, some speculation remains as to whether production quotas will officially change. Despite record crude prices, the past twelve months have seen steady quota levels and the results of this meeting are not expected to buck the trend. Changes in the political climates in these producing countries have recently proven to be far more influential on actual production than the official OPEC quota system. Revisions to quota levels today serve more as an expression of member countries' sentiments regarding global crude oil demand rather than a pricing mechanism.
The graph on the previous page shows the total OPEC crude production level as compared to the official quota level. The quota has remained steady at 28 million barrels per day for the past year, but overall production has been below this level recently. Last month, the OPEC 10 crude oil production was reported by the EIA to be 27.3 million barrels per day. Under or Over The below-quota output is due in part to the fact that countries are not currently able to reach quota levels and spare capacity is limited. The map below shows the total amount of crude oil produced in July 2006, versus their OPEC quotas. Venezuela, Nigeria, Indonesia and Iran are currently producing under their quotas, while the other nations are compensating and producing more.
Indonesia has experienced declining output over the past month to around 890,000 bbl per day. Venezuela and Nigeria have experienced unplanned supply disruptions. It appears that Indonesia will continue to experience an overall decline as little new production comes on line and fields mature. Nigeria has bright prospects in terms of production capacity and reserves but remains hindered by political turmoil. Wild Card As Iraq is not currently under the quota system, their production has not been considered part of OPEC supply. The reality is that this country has been contributing a great deal to world supply, especially in the past few months. In July, Iraq reportedly had production levels around 2.1 million barrels per day down slightly from the 2.2 million barrels per day reported for June. This contributes considerable incremental supply to the market.
OPEC currently contributes 30% of the 85.5 million barrels supplied per day. Regardless of the quota, OPEC producers are an extremely integral component of keeping the world well supplied with crude oil. World crude oil demand remains high, however it is not expected to increase dramatically in the near term.

This phase-out regulation has led to increased ordering at shipyards, but there are several other initiatives that may further increase the price of tankers or keep them at present levels. text:
Protective coatings have traditionally been applied to cargo tanks in vessels that are designed to carry clean products. The newbuilding market is seeing increased interest on coating larger vessels. While many owners are realizing the benefit of coated cargo tanks from a commercial perspective, specifically in the clean product trades, the protective benefits for coated cargo and ballast tanks in crude carriers are also being recognized.
Today, coating of ballast tanks is required according to existing IMO regulations. By mid-2008, the IMO will impose a new set of guidelines to perfect the coating application process known as the Performance Standards for Protective Coating (PSPC.) The standards have been developed in an effort to protect ballast tanks from premature corrosion that can have catastrophic consequences. The PSPC will affect those vessels ordered on or after July 1 st 2008, or for delivery date on or after January 1 st 2012. The primary points of the IMO's regulation are that the coating performance standards should be applied to all ballast and void spaces on all ships, and that the target coating life should be at least 15 years.
Currently, performance standards for cargo tank coatings are under consideration. The IMO expects that coatings will be mandatory on all cargo tanks and ballast tanks on crude and product carriers in the future, and all will be subject to performance standards.
The price of coating a vessel has increased marginally making the incremental cost to an owner an increasingly smaller percentage of the total price of the vessel. Aside from practicalities associated with better protection of the asset, the commercial value of coated cargo tanks will increase as product trades develop in the future. With vessel prices at all time highs, owners are finding it a bit easier to splurge on the coating. With expected increased regulations in the future, owners should find the higher coating costs today a bit easier to justify economically, and in the long term will have a vessel what will be able to better withstand the rigors of worldwide trading.
